newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-NEBIOLO STANDS AT CENTRE OF OLYMPIC SUB-PLOT.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-NEBIOLO STANDS AT CENTRE OF OLYMPIC SUB-PLOT.

text.p: A persistent sub-plot which would have appealed to the dramatists of ancient Greece seethed underneath the sixth edition of the world athletics championships.
The championships concluded on Sunday with the next competition scheduled for Seville in two years' time.
While the youth of the world ran, jumped and threw much as their forebears did in the ancient Olympics the battle to bring the Games back to its spiritual home in 2004 intensified.

At the centre of the drama stood Primo Nebiolo, the Italian lawyer who heads the International Amateur Athletic Federation while simultaneously playing a leading role in the Rome 2004 bidding committee.

Rome and Athens are the favourites among the five bidding cities, especially after the explosion which on Friday destroyed sections of the Olympic stadium in Stockholm, the third European candidate. Cape Town and Buenos Aires are the other bidding cities who learn their fate in Lausanne on September 5.

To help ensure a successful championships, Nebiolo allowed defending champions to take part even if they did not qualify for their national teams, leaving the way clear for double Olympic champion Michael Johnson to compete.
Johnson did not let the IAAF down, overcoming a sudden attack of cramp to win the 400 metres and pick up $60,000 prize money, another innovation at the championships.
For the first time also $100,000 was on the table for any athlete setting a world record but for the first time since the championships started in 1983, no world record was set.
"The level of our world record is very high," Nebiolo said.
"The races are not arranged by the organisers, to break a world record is extremely difficult."

Nebiolo preferred to point instead to the number of countries taking part, a record 200, and to the spreading popularity of the sport. Each of the six world areas -- Africa, Asia, Europe, North and Central America and the Caribbean, Oceania and South America -- produced a medallist at the championships for the first time.
A well-run championships was seen as essential to the Athens bid and the first weekend, featuring the men's and women's 100 metres, must have been an embarrassment to the organisers
Television pictures beamed around the world showed thousands of empty seats and Nebiolo was quick out of the blocks on Monday when asked for his reaction.

"There has maybe not been a great campaign of promotion," Nebiolo said. "Maybe because it was Saturday people in Athens go to the sea...they have the sea all year. They can forget the sea for a week."
Greek Olympic Committee chief Lambis Nikolaou retorted that the programme was too long.
"There are too many days," he said. "Perhaps the prices are too high. At the Olympics there would be lower prices."
The crowds picked up after the weekend and to observers not obsessed with the fate of the 2004 Games the organisation was a success.

One major criticism was the early start times, essential to avoid the worst of the August heat. Several athletes complained and American high hurdles champion Allen Johnson said he had slept with the light on all night before his first round heat to avoid sleeping in.
Gianna Angelopoulos, the formidable lawyer who heads the Greek bid, would not be drawn into any criticism of Nebiolo's dual role and would not comment on any possible conflict of interest.
She did point out that Athens would stage the Olympics later in August in more pleasant weather and promised the notorious Athens' traffic problems would be solved by 2004.
"We are loyal to the Games," she said. "For us the Olympics is a way of life."
In Angelopoulos, Nebiolo may have met his political match. For them both the championships may have ended; the games are just beginning.
